results.question: Compare the disk-induced tidal disruption-driven growth scenario for intermediate-mass black holes described in Rapid Growth of Intermediate-Mass Black Holes through Disk-induced Stellar Disruptions (arXiv:2609.03701v2) with the stellar clustering / bound-companion analysis methods used in Star cluster formation from turbulent clumps. V. Stellar clustering around massive stars (arXiv:2604.27382v2). Specifically: (1) What concrete dTDE mass supply rate and sensitivity to the disk outer radius does the Rapid Growth paper report? (2) What simulation/analysis capabilities from the Star cluster formation paper could be used to test or refine the assumptions about the stellar cusp and bound stellar populations feeding the IMBH in the Rapid Growth paper? Provide an explicit synthesis requiring supported facts from both papers.
results.reference_answer: (1) Rapid Growth of Intermediate-Mass Black Holes through Disk-induced Stellar Disruptions reports that disk-induced stellar disruptions can sustain stellar disruption rates of ~ (1–3) × 10^−3 M☉ yr^−1, and that extending the disk outer radius from R_out = R_sg to R_out = 3 R_sg produces only a slight decrease in the dTDE-driven mass supply (from ~8×10^−4 to ~6×10^−4 M☉ yr^−1), i.e., the overall dTDE rate is only weakly dependent on R_out (evidence: da98ceac0da2dfbc4cb8c97e; 41d12c9455789b742b18e36e). (2) The Star cluster formation from turbulent clumps. V. Stellar clustering around massive stars paper describes N-body models of gradual star cluster formation, post-processing to identify bound systems around massive stars, and constructing projected stellar density profiles to compare clustering predictions with observations (evidence: d26d531b97dd532abb0e07dc; 3f5057c15ab6fdac9f804821). Synthesis: By combining these capabilities, one could supply the Rapid Growth model with more realistic initial conditions for the stellar cusp and local bound-companion population: the clustering paper’s N-body simulations and bound-companion identification methods can quantify the number, radial distribution, and projected density profiles of stars near massive objects at specified cluster ages, which would directly test the Rapid Growth assumption about the available stellar reservoir for disk capture and inward migration. This addresses a limitation noted in Rapid Growth that their simulations model the local dynamical feeding mechanism but require galaxy-scale inputs about the formation and lifetime of gas-rich nuclear environments (da98ceac0da2dfbc4cb8c97e). Together, the Star cluster formation methods could refine the Rapid Growth dTDE supply estimates by providing empirically motivated stellar spatial and dynamical distributions for use in the disk-capture and migration prescriptions (evidence: da98ceac0da2dfbc4cb8c97e; d26d531b97dd532abb0e07dc).

Wang et al. (Rapid Growth...) report measured dTDE mass-supply rates of 7.9 × 10^-4 M⊙ yr^-1 for M• = 3 × 10^3 M⊙, 7.8 × 10^-4 M⊙ yr^-1 for M• = 1 × 10^4 M⊙, and 2.6 × 10^-3 M⊙ yr^-1 for M• = 3 × 10^4 M⊙. [1]

The Rapid Growth paper states that, for IMBH masses within the simulated range (≤ 3 × 10^4 M⊙), they interpolate in log M• – log ṀdTDE using the three discrete measured points. [1]

For black hole masses beyond 3 × 10^4 M⊙, the Rapid Growth paper adopts a conservative constant extrapolated dTDE rate of 2.6 × 10^-4 M⊙ yr^-1. [1]

The Rapid Growth paper reports that the disk-induced disruptions can sustain stellar disruption rates of approximately (1–3) × 10^-3 M⊙ yr^-1, significantly exceeding the Eddington accretion rate for black holes with M• < 10^5 M⊙. [2] [3]

In their rate definition the Rapid Growth paper uses an inner accretion radius R_dTDE = 10^-4 pc as the operational criterion for a dTDE candidate. [4]

The Rapid Growth paper identifies the disk outer radius Rout as a key parameter that determines the reservoir of stars available for capture and tests Rout variations (e.g., Rout = R_sg versus Rout = 3 R_sg) in Figure 8. [2] [5]

Farias et al. (Star cluster formation...) use direct N-body simulations of gradual star-cluster formation (TCCA models) and explicitly state they post-process these N-body simulations to study stellar clustering around massive stars. [6]

The Star cluster formation paper implements a snowballing algorithm to identify bound companions around massive stars (iteratively replacing binaries/triples by their center-of-mass and searching for additional bound companions). [7]

Farias et al. construct projected stellar density profiles around massive stars and report statistics of the number of bound companions ⟨N_bound⟩ as a function of primary mass, cluster mass (M_cl), cloud surface density (Σcloud), companion mass threshold, and star-formation timescale parameters (ε_ff). [7] [8] [9]

Synthesis — To test Rapid Growth’s assumptions about the stellar cusp feeding an IMBH, one should combine the Rapid Growth paper’s measured/interpolated dTDE rates and their explicit dependence on disk outer radius (Rout tests in Figure 8 and the role of Rout as a reservoir parameter) with the Star cluster paper’s outputs: projected stellar density profiles and ⟨N_bound⟩ around massive primaries, the snowballing bound-companion catalogues, and the parameterized runs over M_cl, Σcloud, and ε_ff that change velocity dispersion and companion counts. [1] [2] [5] [7] [8]

Synthesis — Concretely, the cluster outputs to be measured and fed into the dTDE assessment are: local projected stellar density/profile near the IMBH (to map available star number versus radius compared to Rout), the distribution of bound companions and their masses/orbital radii from the snowballing algorithm (to estimate capture supply and survival), and the cluster velocity-dispersion / formation-timescale parameters (ε_ff, M_cl, Σcloud) that alter replenishment rates; these measurements directly map to Rapid Growth’s assumptions about the stellar reservoir, replenishment and the Rout-controlled capture reservoir used to compute ṀdTDE. [1] [5] [7] [8]

The Star cluster formation simulations involve 50% of systems being primordial binaries and include no primordial triples or higher-order multiples. [6]

These limitations are particularly important for interpreting the high-redshift application: our simulations test the local dynamical feeding mechanism, while the formation and lifetime of the required gas-rich nuclear environment must be supplied by galaxy-scale gas inflow, star formation, and feedback. A deeper assessment of how disk-induced TDEs affect seed black hole growth in a cosmological setting will therefore be addressed using cosmological simulations in a companion paper (Wang Z. et al. in preparation), which shows that dTDEs can boost IMBH growth to _∼_ 10[5] _M⊙_ within several tens of millions of years, increasing the abundance of massive black holes at _z ∼_ 9–10 and partially alleviating the tension with JWST-discovered overmassive candidates.

Wang et al. 

2 

disk interactions can act as a dissipative conveyor of stellar material: the disk captures stars from a threedimensional cluster, damps their orbits, and delivers them inward on a migration timescale. 

This mechanism is especially relevant for intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs). For _M•_ ≲ 10[5] _M⊙_ , the dTDE mass supply rate can exceed the Eddington-limited gas accretion rate, and may therefore dominate the early mass budget of the black hole. The problem is not simply whether an individual star can be captured by the disk; that can be estimated from local drag and migration timescales. The central question is whether a realistic collisional stellar cluster can maintain a continuous supply of stars to the disk after the innermost stars have been consumed. The answer depends on several coupled processes: the formation of a stellar cusp around the IMBH, two-body relaxation that refills the disk-crossing population, stochastic few-body encounters, mass segregation and stellar evolution, and physical collisions among stars that captured by the disk. These effects determine both the dTDE rate and the mass spectrum of the disrupted stars.

retrieved_chunks.text: _Limitations and future work._ —Despite the insights provided by our simulations, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the conversion efficiency of disrupted stellar mass into black hole growth remains uncertain. Radiative hydrodynamic simulations of classical TDEs suggest accreted fractions of _∼_ 25%–43% for a 10[6] _M⊙_ SMBH disrupting stars of 1–300 _M⊙_ (Bu et al. 2023; Sheng et al. 2026). In our disk-induced TDE scenario, however, stars are delivered on nearly circular, coplanar orbits and migrate inward through the disk prior to disruption. This may lead to more efficient debris circularization and thus a potentially higher accreted fraction than that achieved in the highly eccentric, parabolic orbits typical of classical TDEs. Nevertheless, our current assumption of full accretion should be regarded as an optimistic upper limit. Second, the limited duration of our simulations raises the question of whether the seemingly steady dTDE rate measured over _∼_ 0.3 Myr can be sustained over 30 Myr required to grow an IMBH to _∼_ 10[5] _M⊙_ . This would require both a continuous external gas supply to maintain the disk and a sufficiently large stellar reservoir, from which stars can be continuously replenished into the diskcrossing region via two-body scattering among stars and dynamical friction against the ambient gas over long timescales ( _>_ 30 Myr). Third, our analytic treatment of star–disk interactions, while capturing the essential physics, omits important processes associated with embedded stars, such as gas accretion onto stars and stellar remnants, stellar winds, supernovae, and their feedback on the disk structure. ## 4. CONCLUSIONS AND DISCUSSIONS In this work, we investigate dTDEs as a stellar feeding channel for IMBHs embedded in gas-rich dense nuclear star clusters. By performing high-precision direct _N_ - body simulations with analytic prescriptions for star– disk interactions, we follow the coupled evolution of the stellar cusp, relaxation-driven replenishment, disk capture, inward migration, stellar mergers, and eventual accretion onto the central IMBH. We find that this process can sustain stellar disruption rates of _∼_ (1 _−_ 3) _×_ 10 _[−]_[3] _M⊙_ yr _[−]_[1] , significantly exceeding the Eddington accretion rate for black holes with _M• <_ 10[5] _M⊙_ . The main conclusion is therefore that disk-induced stellar disruptions can provide an efficient and dynamically sustained stellar mass supply to IMBHs in compact gasrich stellar systems. ## 3.3. _Rate of disk-induced TDE_ 

In this subsection, we use the crossing of the inner accretion radius, _R_ dTDE = 10 _[−]_[4] pc, as the operational definition of a dTDE candidate. This radius connects the local orbital outcome of star–disk interactions to the global feeding rate of the IMBH. The disruption rate is not set only by the instantaneous number of stars inside the disk. It is controlled by a sequence of linked processes: stars must first be supplied to disk-crossing orbits by the collisional cluster, then dissipatively captured or driven inward by the disk, and finally avoid being scattered or collisionally removed before reaching _R_ dTDE.

As a first step, we have performed simulations for only three discrete IMBH masses, from which we measure the˙ dTDE rates: _M_ dTDE = 7 _._ 9 _×_ 10 _[−]_[4] _M⊙_ yr _[−]_[1] for _M•_ = 3 _×_ 10[3] _M⊙_ , 7 _._ 8 _×_ 10 _[−]_[4] _M⊙_ yr _[−]_[1] for _M•_ = 1 _×_ 10[4] _M⊙_ , and 2 _._ 6 _×_ 10 _[−]_[3] _M⊙_ yr _[−]_[1] for _M•_ = 3 _×_ 10[4] _M⊙_ (see Figure 7). For IMBH masses within this range, we employ linear interpolation in the log _M•_ –log _M_[˙] dTDE plane based on these three data points. For black hole masses beyond 3 _×_ 10[4] _M⊙_ , we adopt a constant dTDE rate of 2 _._ 6 _×_ 10 _[−]_[4] _M⊙_ yr _[−]_[1] as a conservative extrapolation. This assumption is motivated by two physical considerations. First, the dTDE rate is not expected to increase indefinitely with black hole mass. As the black hole becomes more massive, the timescale for capturing stars through star–disk interactions becomes longer, preventing a continuous increase of the dTDE rate with black hole mass (Wang et al. 2024c). Second, the Eddington accretion rate of the surrounding gas disk increases with black hole mass, eventually making gas accretion the dominant growth channel and reducing the relative contribution of dTDEs (see Kennedy et al. 2016).

## **2.1 Star Cluster Formation Simulations** 

In this work, we use the Turbulent Clump Core Accretion (TCCA) star cluster formation models developed by Farias et al. (2017, 2019); Farias & Tan (2023), where star clusters are formed inside magnetized, turbulent, gravitationally bound, and initially starless clumps within giant molecular clouds (GMCs). These consist of a suite of unique _𝑁_ -body simulations focused on accurately following stellar dynamics in the early stages of star cluster formation, i.e., where there is still ongoing formation of stars. These models assume individual stars and primordial binary stars form via stochastic core accretion with initial clump properties based on the Turbulent Core Accretion (TCA) model (McKee & Tan 2003). Farias et al. (2017) (hereafter, Paper I) presented the extreme case of instantaneous star cluster formation, where all stars are formed together at once and remaining gas is assumed to leave the system instantaneously according to a given global star formation efficiency (SFE, _𝜖_ ). Farias et al. (2019) and Farias & Tan (2023) (hereafter, Papers II and III, respectively) presented the case of gradual star cluster formation. In these simulations, we assume that a fraction ( _𝜖_ ) of the gas is gradually converted into stars while the remaining gas is also steadily removed from the system due to stellar feedback. This is modeled as a linear decrease of the gas reservoir (Equation 9, Paper III) until it reaches zero at the end of star formation, _𝑡★_ . The timescale over which this process occurs is set by the star formation efficiency per free-fall time, _𝜖_ ff, such that higher values of _𝜖_ ff result in shorter _𝑡★_ (see Paper III for details). The case of _𝜖_ ff = ∞ corresponds to the instantaneous case where all stars are formed at once, whereas the slowest case considered assumes _𝜖_ ff = 0.01. For this paper, we post-processed clusters formed from _𝑁_ -body models outlined in Paper III.

Massive stars are formed randomly in the star cluster, i.e., approximating the process of Turbulent Core Accretion in the limit of no primordial mass segregation of massive star formation. We perform an analysis of clustering of companions around these massive stars. We also compare with observations and massive stars formed by Competitive Accretion in `STARFORGE` simulations. In addition, the simulations involve 50% of systems being primordial binaries, but with no preference for massive stars to be favored as being in multiples. There are no primordial triples or higher-order multiples, so such systems must form dynamically during the evolution of the cluster. We track the formation of such bound systems of companions around massive stars to study the effect of star cluster environment on the dynamical capture of companions. This exploration yields benchmark statistics that can be used to compare the results of more sophisticated MHD + _𝑁_ -body simulations to be developed in future studies.

## **5 CONCLUSIONS** 

Anosova J. P., 1986, Ap&SS, 124, 217 

- Appel S. M., et al., 2026, AJ, 172, 12 

In this paper, we studied the clustering of bound and unbound companions around massive stars inside gradually forming star clusters via “Turbulent Clump Core Accretion” (TCCA) by post-processing existing _𝑁_ −body simulations. In these simulations, star clusters are formed in different formation timescales ( _𝑡★_ ) parameterized by star formation efficiency per freefall time ( _𝜖_ ff), mass of star-forming clump ( _𝑀_ cl) and mass surface densities (Σcloud) of the parent cloud. 

We found that massive stars in the center of bound cluster gather more companions than massive stars that have been ejected from the cluster. We found that ejected stars are mostly single or in binaries. The number of companions is greater for massive stars in star clusters with lower stellar velocity dispersion and higher stellar densities. When we compared the clustering of companions around our massive stars with projected stellar density profiles, we found a good match to YSO profiles in the AFGL 5180 and G19.88-0.53 star-forming regions. Finally, we noted a lack of close triple companions around our simulated O-stars when compared to companions around O-stars in the `SMASH+` survey. Since these companions were not captured dynamically, they are likely formed via primordial routes like core or disk fragmentation. 

In the future, we aim to extend our gradual star cluster formation models with hydrodynamical coupling and an accurate treatment of primordial triples. We are also currently working on extending the analysis of dynamically gathered companions around primary stars across the full stellar mass spectrum.

## **2.2 Clustering around Massive Stars** 

We examine the stellar clustering around massive stars (≥ 8 _𝑀_ ⊙) formed in our simulations. To study the effect of cluster environment on such clustering, we divide these massive stars into three different subsets according to their location and boundedness. First, we determine stars that are bound to the star cluster using a snowballing algorithm developed in Farias & Tan (2023). Then, we refer bound massive stars in the central regions within 20% of the half-mass radius of their star cluster as _central stars_ . Similarly, massive stars beyond 20% of the half-mass radius which are in the outer regions of the star cluster are referred as _offset stars_ . Finally, massive stars that are unbound from the star cluster are referred to as _ejected stars_ . 

After dividing massive stars into subsets, we study the properties of bound and unbound companions around them. For this purpose, we have developed routines to identify bound companions around any given massive star. The routine works as follows: First, we identify the closest bound companion (a binary partner) to the massive star. Then, we replace the two stars with a center of mass particle. Next, we search for the next closest star that is bounded to this center of mass particle, hence forming a triple. If present, we replace the triple with its corresponding center of mass particle. Then, we search for the next closest bound companion. We perform this process iteratively to identify all the stars that are bound to the massive star. We start this search around the most massive star, identify its bound companions and tag them. Then, we move to the next most massive untagged star and search for its bound companions, ensuring there is no doublecounting of stars during this iterative process. This allows us to identify all the bound stars that are centered on independent primary massive stars within our star cluster.

_Accretion Disk Model_ —The outer radius of the accretion disk, _R_ out, is a key parameter that determines the reservoir of stars available for capture. Theoretically, the disk structure is expected to consist of an inner, gravitationally stable standard accretion disk and an outer, marginally unstable star-forming disk (Sirko & Goodman 2003; Thompson et al. 2005; Dittmann & Miller 2020). As gas flows from galactic scales toward the central SMBH, the increasing density can drive the disk toward gravitational instability and fragmentation, triggering star formation. Feedback from newly formed stars (e.g., radiation and supernova explosions) can heat the gas and regulate further fragmentation, maintaining the disk in a marginally stable state with _Q ∼_ 1. The remaining gas continues to flow inward, feeding the inner accretion disk. However, the outer extent of this starforming disk remains uncertain. Observations of nearby AGNs have not yet provided clear evidence for such an extended component, while recent JWST observations of “little red dots” with characteristic V-shaped spectra have been suggested as possible candidates for systems containing such compact star-forming disks in the early Universe (Zhang et al. 2026; Chen et al. 2026).

## **2 METHODS** 

In section 2.1, we describe the _𝑁_ -body models of gradual star cluster formation used for this paper. We have post-processed these simulations to study the evolution of stellar clustering around massive stars. In section 2.2, we describe the process of identifying bound systems around massive stars, which are later compared to study how the environment and formation timescale affect these bound systems. In section 2.3, we describe how we construct projected stellar density profiles around massive stars to compare different models of massive star formation with each other and with observations.

claims.text: Wang et al. (Rapid Growth...) report measured dTDE mass-supply rates of 7.9 × 10^-4 M⊙ yr^-1 for M• = 3 × 10^3 M⊙, 7.8 × 10^-4 M⊙ yr^-1 for M• = 1 × 10^4 M⊙, and 2.6 × 10^-3 M⊙ yr^-1 for M• = 3 × 10^4 M⊙.
The Rapid Growth paper states that, for IMBH masses within the simulated range (≤ 3 × 10^4 M⊙), they interpolate in log M• – log ṀdTDE using the three discrete measured points.
For black hole masses beyond 3 × 10^4 M⊙, the Rapid Growth paper adopts a conservative constant extrapolated dTDE rate of 2.6 × 10^-4 M⊙ yr^-1.

The Rapid Growth paper reports that the disk-induced disruptions can sustain stellar disruption rates of approximately (1–3) × 10^-3 M⊙ yr^-1, significantly exceeding the Eddington accretion rate for black holes with M• < 10^5 M⊙.
In their rate definition the Rapid Growth paper uses an inner accretion radius R_dTDE = 10^-4 pc as the operational criterion for a dTDE candidate.

The Rapid Growth paper identifies the disk outer radius Rout as a key parameter that determines the reservoir of stars available for capture and tests Rout variations (e.g., Rout = R_sg versus Rout = 3 R_sg) in Figure 8.

Farias et al. (Star cluster formation...) use direct N-body simulations of gradual star-cluster formation (TCCA models) and explicitly state they post-process these N-body simulations to study stellar clustering around massive stars.

The Star cluster formation paper implements a snowballing algorithm to identify bound companions around massive stars (iteratively replacing binaries/triples by their center-of-mass and searching for additional bound companions).

Farias et al. construct projected stellar density profiles around massive stars and report statistics of the number of bound companions ⟨N_bound⟩ as a function of primary mass, cluster mass (M_cl), cloud surface density (Σcloud), companion mass threshold, and star-formation timescale parameters (ε_ff).

Synthesis — To test Rapid Growth’s assumptions about the stellar cusp feeding an IMBH, one should combine the Rapid Growth paper’s measured/interpolated dTDE rates and their explicit dependence on disk outer radius (Rout tests in Figure 8 and the role of Rout as a reservoir parameter) with the Star cluster paper’s outputs: projected stellar density profiles and ⟨N_bound⟩ around massive primaries, the snowballing bound-companion catalogues, and the parameterized runs over M_cl, Σcloud, and ε_ff that change velocity dispersion and companion counts.

Synthesis — Concretely, the cluster outputs to be measured and fed into the dTDE assessment are: local projected stellar density/profile near the IMBH (to map available star number versus radius compared to Rout), the distribution of bound companions and their masses/orbital radii from the snowballing algorithm (to estimate capture supply and survival), and the cluster velocity-dispersion / formation-timescale parameters (ε_ff, M_cl, Σcloud) that alter replenishment rates; these measurements directly map to Rapid Growth’s assumptions about the stellar reservoir, replenishment and the Rout-controlled capture reservoir used to compute ṀdTDE.
The Star cluster formation simulations involve 50% of systems being primordial binaries and include no primordial triples or higher-order multiples.

The provided quoted texts match each factual claim precisely.
